content.thinking:
I'm examining the error logs around the incident—ClientDisconnected rates stayed similar before and after, error rate warnings were slightly elevated afterward, and account pages rendered normally at 21:53 with no reported customer loss. This suggests the issue may not have had a visible customer-facing impact.

The symptom seems to be that nobody using the shop noticed anything wrong, but the shop's metrics stopped arriving entirely. Tracing the cause: the ServiceMonitor selects the scrape endpoint by the port name "metrics," but the running revision actually names it "http-metrics," so the mismatch broke scraping without affecting actual service traffic.

I'm tracing this back to a deploy at P2 that renamed ports to match platform convention without updating scrape.yaml, and confirming that metrics were still flowing fine between the earlier P1 deploy and the actual onset — ruling P1 out as the cause since metrics data existed right up until the point things broke.

The real mechanism is that the ServiceMonitor selects by name "metrics," but the rename changed it to "http-metrics," and since a mismatched name isn't treated as an error, the scrape config just silently returns an empty target list. The contributing gap is that nothing validates the two names agree, and the rename was only applied to the values file while scrape.yaml was left untouched — that's the full causal chain I want to lay out from symptom to mechanism to root change.

Now I'm identifying contributing factors: CF-1 is the missing consistency check between the scrape port name and values file port name, which would have caught this before deploy, and this gets addressed by the fix that adds a test — though whether CI actually runs that test is still unclear, so I should propose gating deploys on it.

CF-2 is that a ServiceMonitor port mismatch isn't an error — it silently produces an empty target list, so detection only happened via the MetricsAbsent alert minutes later. An alert on an empty scrape target set could have caught this faster at deploy time. There's also the fact that nobody was paged since there was no linked on-call incident, suggesting a paging gap that may have delayed human action during escalation.

The deeper root cause is that the platform-wide naming convention rename didn't include the scrape config, pointing to a cross-file coupling issue — templating the ServiceMonitor port from a single metrics.portName source would prevent future drift between the two files.

Also, revision c3c36da running now isn't in main's history, so the branch it came from needs the same one-line scrape port fix applied and a new revision deployed carrying it; merging the fix into main alone won't change what's actually running until a deploy picks it up. Until that happens, the shop's metrics stay uncollected, meaning any real fault there would go undetected by metrics-based alerts.

For the lessons, I'm noting what went well: Argus correctly tied the service stop to the deploy and read the diff shortly after the alert, Code-Fix proposed a draft PR promptly, and Argus rightly declined to roll back what was an intentional change.

For what went wrong, I'm weighing whether the real issue is that the rename shipped to production without updating the scrape config, and noting that Code-Fix's fix targets main rather than the actual running revision, so merging it alone wouldn't restore metrics — the branch with the running commit needs the same fix. I'm also flagging a bit of luck: the rename also touched web and admin port names, so if anything else had been routing or probing by the old names, shoppers could have actually been affected.

I'll keep the second point and note my assumption rests on the comment in scrape.yaml rather than a directly observed target list, since nothing confirms the empty list was actually read. In plain words: a port renaming done for naming-convention reasons wasn't reflected in the separate scrape config, so monitoring had nothing to collect from — the root cause traces to the ServiceMonitor definition in deploy/scrape.yaml.

The ServiceMonitor selects by the port name `metrics`, but a later revision renamed it to `http-metrics` in values-production.yaml, and since a mismatched port name isn't flagged as an error, Prometheus silently ended up with an empty target list. I'll steer away from citing specific numbers like revision hashes or PR numbers directly, referring to things like "the draft pull request" instead, and keep any timing references as placeholders in the steps.

I'm ruling out the P1 hypothesis based on earlier evidence, and noting flags without restating the still-valid mechanism from C2 since it hasn't been refuted. For action items, I'm separating the fix into two distinct steps: first, making the same one-line scrape port correction on the branch that the problematic revision originated from, and second, deploying a revision carrying that change — keeping "confirm metrics resume" as a separate concern rather than folding it into the deploy step.

For prevention, I want the ServiceMonitor's port to be derived directly from metrics.portName so the two values can't diverge, and I want the port-name consistency test added to the gating checks for deploys. For detection, I'd alert when the io-shop ServiceMonitor has no scrape targets, and for process, route the MetricsAbsent alert to on-call and add monitoring configs like ServiceMonitors to the checklist for the estate-wide port-naming rollout, since that's likely where the gap originated.

I'm now reconsidering CF-2: the issue is that an empty target list from a mismatched port name doesn't surface as its own error -- it only gets caught once MetricsAbsent's wait period passes, which delayed detection. I'm debating whether to fold that into root cause or keep it as a separate contributing factor about missing alerting on empty scrape targets, but I'll keep root cause focused and treat this as its own factor.

For CF-3, paging matters: if someone had been paged, they'd have picked up the fix and redeployed sooner. That settles the factors, so now I'll write it up.

action_items.item: Make the same one-line change to deploy/scrape.yaml (port `http-metrics`) on the branch that revision c3c36da was deployed from, which is not in main's history.
Deploy to io-shop a revision that carries the scrape port change.
Render the ServiceMonitor's endpoint port from `metrics.portName` in the values file so the two cannot drift apart.
Run the port-name consistency test from the draft fix as a required check on changes to the deploy/ directory.
Add an alert that fires when the io-shop ServiceMonitor selects no scrape targets.
Route MetricsAbsent alerts on io-shop to the on-call page.

causal_chain.step: Nobody using the shop saw anything wrong. Instead, the shop's metrics stopped arriving from {metrics_stopped_at}, and MetricsAbsent fired.

The metrics stopped because Prometheus had nothing to scrape. In the running revision, the ServiceMonitor selects the endpoint by the port name `metrics`, but the values file names the metrics port `http-metrics`. A name that matches no port is not an error to the operator: it gives a target list with nothing in it.

ruled_out.what: The earlier deploy of revision 2c8f731: the shop's metrics were still being collected with it in place, up to the minute before the onset.
A feature-flag change: the flag provider shows no flag changes by anyone but Argus in the hour before it was read.

causal_chain.step: The names disagree because the deploy of revision c3c36da at {P2.1} renamed every port to the platform convention (web to http, admin to http-admin, metrics to http-metrics) in deploy/values-production.yaml. That is the only file its diff lists, so deploy/scrape.yaml still selects `metrics`. As of {T13.1}, all {T13.2} replicas ran that revision.

input.cause_in_plain_words: A planned renaming of the shop's network connection points, made to follow a platform-wide naming convention, was not carried into the separate setting that tells the monitoring system where to collect the shop's measurements, so the monitoring system found nothing to collect.

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing checks that the port name in deploy/scrape.yaml matches `metrics.portName` in deploy/values-production.yaml (the scrape file says so itself). No check of the rename against the scrape configuration was seen before the deploy.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The mismatch would have been caught before the rename reached production, and the metrics would not have stopped.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No alert was seen for the shop's ServiceMonitor selecting no scrape targets. The fault was found only by MetricsAbsent, which waits for a stretch with no samples.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The empty target list would have been flagged as soon as the deploy landed, not only after the absence window had passed.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: MetricsAbsent on io-shop did not page anyone: no on-call incident was linked to the alert.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have known straight away that the shop was unwatched and could have pushed the scrape fix through to a deploy sooner.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

got_lucky: The shop kept no metrics for the whole stretch. Had it actually broken during that time, nothing watching its metrics would have shown it or alerted on it.
went_well: Argus read the diff of the suspect deploy {T12.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, and tied the stopped metrics to the port rename.
Argus declined to roll back the rename, because undoing it would reverse a change made on purpose. It sent the incident on toward a fix instead.
Code-Fix opened a draft pull request {T20.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised. It changes the scrape's port name and adds a test that keeps the two files in step.
went_wrong: Code-Fix wrote its fix against main, which does not contain the running revision. Merging it will not bring the metrics back until a deploy carries the change, and the branch that revision c3c36da came from needs the same change before it is deployed again.

input.root_cause: The ServiceMonitor in deploy/scrape.yaml picks the endpoint to scrape by the port name `metrics`. Revision c3c36da renamed that port to `http-metrics` in deploy/values-production.yaml and left the scrape file alone. A ServiceMonitor port name that matches no port is not an error to the operator, so Prometheus was left with an empty target list and collected nothing from the shop.
input.still_at_risk: The scrape was still looking for a port name the running revision no longer has, so any real trouble in the shop would go unseen by anything that watches its metrics until a deploy brings the two names back into line.
input.symptom: Nobody using the shop saw anything wrong; the shop's metrics stopped arriving.
